title: Service Posture and Capacity Playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview:

This playbook defines a unified approach to measuring and managing service posture for Redwood Inference services (hosted API, serving runtime, routing, cache layer). It consolidates SLOs and error-budget handling, capacity planning principles, incident review standards, operational tooling, and a set of canonical runbooks. The goal is to make reliability predictable and actionable for engineers and oncall personnel.

Scope:

- Applies to production-facing inference services and control-plane components used in customer inference routing (api-gateway, runtime, cache-store, scheduler).
- Not in scope: CI systems, developer tooling, internal analytics that do not affect customer-facing SLOs.

Key concepts and definitions:

- Service Posture Index (SPI): a single-number indicator (0-100) combining availability, latency, and error-budget health to summarize operational posture. SPI is intended for executive dashboards, oncall briefing, and automated escalation rules.
- Error budget: remaining allowed unreliability within an SLO window (typically 30d). Burn rates are monitored daily for escalation.
- Headroom: planned spare capacity to tolerate spikes and failures (expressed as a percent of total capacity).

Service Posture Index (SPI) calculation (summary):

SPI = 100 - (A_penalty + L_penalty + EB_penalty)

- A_penalty: availability shortfall mapped to 0-40. (Example: if availability < target by 0.05% → scaled penalty).
- L_penalty: latency degradation mapped to 0-30 based on p95/p99 breach severity.
- EB_penalty: error-budget burn rate mapped to 0-30 where elevated burn (>10x baseline) contributes maximal penalty.

SPI usage guidance:

1) SPI >= 90: green posture; normal operations.
2) SPI 75-89: advisory; investigate trends, consider modest traffic shaping.
3) SPI 60-74: action required; open a reliability ticket, pull capacity, and prepare fallback plans.
4) SPI < 60: critical; trigger incident process and consider emergency mitigations (model fallbacks, route to Dedicated pools, degrade non-critical features).

SLO and Error Budget Matrix (canonical defaults):

Service | SLI | SLO target (30d) | Measurement window | Burn-rate trigger (daily) | Primary owner | Runbook
---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---
api-gateway | request success (5xx+client errors excluded) | 99.95% | rolling 30d | >3% of budget/day | runtime-eng | /runbooks/api-gateway-failure
text-generation-runtime | availability (model respond) + p95 latency | 99.9% availability, p95 < 350ms | rolling 30d | >2% budget/day OR p95 > 350ms sustained 30m | serving-runtime | /runbooks/runtime-degradation
kv-cache | get/put success & median read latency | 99.99% | rolling 30d | >1% budget/day | infra-storage | /runbooks/cache-throttle
router | routing success & TTL fallbacks | 99.95% | rolling 30d | >3% budget/day | platform-routing | /runbooks/router-fallback

Operational notes on SLOs and SLIs:

- SLIs must be implemented as near-source metrics (nginx/gRPC proxy, runtime telemetry) and exported to Prometheus. Avoid synthetic-only SLIs for primary measurement.
- Measurement window is rolling 30d for customer-facing availability; separate 7d window used for urgent escalations and burn-rate smoothing.
- All SLOs and SLI definitions live in the metrics repo under infrastructure/observability/slo-defs (reference ID: SLO-REPO-1).

Capacity planning principles and thresholds:

Principles:
- Target utilization band: 55-70% steady-state on serving-pool GPUs to preserve headroom for spikes and model warm-up penalties.
- Buffering pathways: maintain token-queue limits that ensure 99th percentile queue latency < 200ms at target utilization.
- Progressive scaling over-provisioning: autoscale triggers are conservative by default to reduce oscillation. Manual scale increments are used for predictable events (product launches, benchmark demos).

Capacity matrix (example for popular instance types):

Component | Metric | Baseline capacity unit | Nominal throughput per unit | Target util | Safe headroom
---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:
text-runtime (A100-80GB) | tokens/sec | 1 GPU | 18k tokens/s (avg mixture) | 60% | 40% spare
text-runtime (H100-80GB) | tokens/sec | 1 GPU | 26k tokens/s | 60% | 40% spare
embeddings (A10G) | requests/sec | 1 GPU | 120 req/s (avg vectors) | 65% | 35% spare
cache-store | ops/sec | 1 shard | 20k reads/s | 70% | 30% spare

Capacity runbooks and planning cadence:

- Quarterly capacity review owned by eng-sre (capacity review doc) with input from product and sales forecasting.
- Pre-launch checklist (2 weeks before traffic event): traffic forecast, required capacity delta, runbook author, rollback criteria, canary configuration.
- Emergency capacity expansion: oncall may request burst capacity from cloud infra runbook; approval flow: oncall -> infra-ops -> SRE lead. Aim for < 2 hours for urgent expansion.

Autoscaling and throttling policy (summary):

1) Target-based autoscaler uses 5m average CPU and request-concurrency signals. Scale-up threshold: sustained 70% target metric for 10m. Scale-down: <50% for 15m.
2) If error-budget burn exceeds 8% daily, autoscaler moves to conservative mode (no scale-down actions for next 4h).
3) Global throttles: route-level token-bucket limits defined per-customer SKU; automatic soft-degradation routes non-critical routes to low-cost model variant when p95 breach persists > 20m.

Incident review standard and post-incident process:

Goals: produce blameless, actionable reviews, surface remediation, and close the loop with product owners.

Timeline and roles:
- Incident declared: incident commander (IC) assigned; oncall documents timeline and mitigations.
- 72h: initial incident triage note published to Slack + incident channel.
- 7 days: post-incident review draft (owner: IC) with timeline, impact, detection, and short-term mitigations.
- 14 days: final postmortem published, including root cause, action items, severity scoring, and verification plan. Each action item must have an owner and due date.

Postmortem required sections (minimum):
1) Summary and impact (customer-visible effects, estimated requests affected)
2) Timeline of events (UTC timestamps)
3) Detection and tooling that alerted (links to Grafana/Alerts)
4) Root cause analysis (why the bug/issue happened)
5) Remediation and permanent fixes
6) Action items (owner + ETA)
7) Test/verification plan and follow-up date

Severity and follow-up rules:
- Sev-1 incidents require a written postmortem published within 14 days and a follow-up verification within 30 days.
- All Sev-1/Sev-2 action items must be tracked in the reliability backlog and assigned priority P1/P2.

Operational tooling and dashboard mapping:

Primary tools: Prometheus (SLI scrape and raw metrics), Cortex for long-term TSDB, Grafana (dashboards), Alertmanager (routing to PagerDuty), Honeycomb (trace analysis), Datadog (ingest-heavy telemetry), Slack (incident channels), Jira (action items).

Canonical dashboards and their owners:

- SPI Executive (grafana): owner eng-sre/observability
- Runtime Health (grafana): p95/p99, concurrency, GPU utilization; owner serving-runtime team
- Error-Budget Details (grafana): per-SLO burn-rate charts; owner eng-sre
- Capacity Forecast (custom sheet + grafana): headroom and trend; owner capacity-planning subgroup

Alerting hygiene checklist:
1) Alerts map directly to SLO burn or to actionable recovery steps (avoid noise).
2) Alert severity corresponds to escalations (pagerduty routing rules defined in Alertmanager).
3) Every fired page must create an incident channel and a temporary hypothesis thread.

Runbooks (selected canonical procedures):

Runbook: runtime-degradation (high-level)
- Trigger: p95 > 350ms sustained for 30m OR SPI < 75.
- Steps:
  1) Verify Grafana charts for increased CPU/GPU queue/backpressure and check traces (Honeycomb) for hot-keys.
  2) Check model memory pressure (kubectl top pods -l app=runtime) and KV cache miss rates.
  3) If memory pressure high: evict non-critical models, roll to smaller batch size (config: serving.runtime.batch_size -> 4).
  4) Route traffic to warm Dedicated pools via routing rule: rctl route set --service runtime --target dedicated-pool-v2 --weight 30%.
  5) If degradation persists for 20m: enable model fallback (route to quantized model variant) and escalate to oncall lead.

Runbook: api-gateway-5xx-spike
- Trigger: 5xx spike > 0.5% for 10m or availability breach for 5m
- Steps:
  1) Verify upstream runtime health and throttles.
  2) Rollback recent gateway config changes (git rev-list and oks: gateway-config rollback --to <commit>).
  3) If rollback not possible, flip to maintenance routing: set maintenance header and return 503 for non-critical paths.

Example SLO config (YAML snippet for metrics repo):

"""yaml
slo:
  name: text-generation-runtime-availability
  sli:
    type: ratio
    success: "http_status < 500 and not client_error"
    total: "requests"
  target: 0.999
  window: 30d
  owner: serving-runtime
  alerting:
    burn_rate_fast: 5.0   # 5x burn rate triggers immediate page
    burn_rate_slow: 2.0   # 2x burn rate sends advisory
"""

Operational best practices and templates:

- Every new service must provide SLI definitions and a basic Grafana dashboard before public launch.
- Keep runbooks under 10 steps with explicit rollback points.
- Use synthetic load tests in staging that mimic 99th percentile latencies before scheduling production traffic increases.

Ownership and governance:

- eng-sre owns SPI definition, alerting routing, and incident review standard.
- Team owners (serving-runtime, platform-routing, infra-storage) own SLOs for their services and must participate in quarterly capacity reviews.
- Product & Sales input is required for forecasted growth that affects capacity in the next quarter.

Appendix: quick commands and useful links

- Check SLO burn rates: curl -s "https://metrics.internal/api/slo/burn?service=text-runtime" | jq .
- Hot traces (Honeycomb): https://honeycomb.redwood/company/runtime-traces
- Grafana SPI dashboard: https://grafana.redwood/d/SPI
- Escalation PagerDuty: https://pagerduty.redwood/services/eng-sre-primary
